title: Negative space — Image Wiki
text:
Negative space
  The empty parts of an image are shapes too, and you are composing them whether you notice or not.

  
    Termnegative space
    Also calledwhite space, empty space, ground, breathing room, passive space
    Not the same asfigure-ground, minimalism, depth of field
    Read8 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Why it happensWhat negative space doesWorking space versus an under-filled frameAcross different mediaCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Look at the NBC logo. Six coloured feathers arranged in a fan — and a white peacock standing in the middle of them, made of nothing at all. Nobody drew that bird. The gap between the feathers is the bird.
That is the whole idea in one image. The empty parts of a picture have shapes, those shapes are visible, and they are doing work. Negative space is the name for the parts your eye files as "not the object": sky, wall, water, shadow, blur, floor. Positive space is the object.
The trap in the word "empty" is that it sounds like nothing is happening there. Something is always happening there. The only question is whether anyone chose it.
Why it happens
Before you can recognise anything in an image, your visual system has to split it into figure and ground — which regions are objects and which are the stuff objects sit on. This happens in the first moments of looking, ahead of naming anything (SRC-028).
Two things about that split matter for judging pictures.
It is mutually exclusive. A region is figure or it is ground, never both at once.



Rubin's vase, after Edgar Rubin's 1915 figure. Drawing by Ian Remsen via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.
There is exactly one boundary in this picture and it does two jobs. Read the black as figure and you get two faces nose to nose. Read the white as figure and you get a stemmed vase. The pixels never change.
What you cannot do is hold both readings at once — try, and it flips. Neither reading is wrong; your visual system simply refuses to assign one contour to two objects simultaneously, and it will not let you opt out of choosing.


It is decided by cues you do not control. The smaller of two overlapping regions tends to become the figure. Convex shapes become figure more readily than concave ones. Enclosed regions become figure. If your subject happens to be the larger, flatter, more concave region, the background will take the figure role and your subject will read as a hole (SRC-028).
Because the split is forced, the leftover region has a definite outline. Photographers and designers talk about the shape between two people, the shape of sky between two branches, the wedge of pavement in the bottom corner. Those shapes are as visible as the objects, and an ugly one is as noticeable as an ugly object.
Smashing's series puts the design version bluntly: space is an active element, not a passive background (SRC-029). Brejon, coming from film lighting, treats figure/ground and negative space as the same topic (SRC-098).
What negative space does
It raises the apparent importance of what is left. Fewer things present means each present thing counts for more. Space around an object is also what makes it read as isolated, and isolation is one of the strongest ways to make something the focal point. See Visual hierarchy.



Caspar David Friedrich, The Monk by the Sea, 1808–10 (Alte Nationalgalerie, Berlin). Public domain.
Three horizontal bands and one vertical mark. The sky takes roughly the top three quarters of the canvas, the sea is a narrow dark strip, and the pale shore fills the bottom. The only interruption anywhere is the monk — a dark upright taking up under a tenth of the picture's height, on a canvas 1.7 metres across.
Measure how little he is given and how much he gets: no detail, no face, no colour, no light on him. What makes him the subject is that he is the single event in an otherwise unbroken field, and that the two largest shapes in the picture have no other business.
This is also the cleanest test of the "empty space is wasted space" instinct. Crop to the monk and the shore and you still have a competent small picture of a figure on a beach. You have thrown away the entire meaning.


It gives the eye somewhere to rest. Space between groups is what lets you see them as groups at all — the same mechanism as the gap between paragraphs. Remove all of it and the image becomes an even field of stuff with no entry point (SRC-029).
It gives direction somewhere to go. If a subject faces or moves to the left, the space usually wants to be on the left. Photographers call this the rule of space: leave room for the subject to look into or run into (SRC-024). A bird about to launch, with a stretch of sky in front of it, reads as about to. The same bird cropped tight against the front edge reads as blocked.
It creates tension when you take it away. Crowding a subject against an edge is uncomfortable, which is exactly why it is useful for claustrophobia, confinement, pressure. Reverse the rule of space deliberately — put the empty space behind the moving subject — and you get a sense of something closing in.



Hokusai, The Great Wave off Kanagawa, c. 1831. The famous part is the wave. The reason it works is everything that is not the wave.
Look at the hollow between the crest and the boats — a large, clean, almost featureless shape. It is doing as much work as the wave: it is the only quiet area in the picture, so the eye rests there, and resting there is what makes you notice Mount Fuji sitting small in the gap. Fuji gets no detail and no contrast. It gets space, and space is enough.
Then cover the pale sky in the upper right with your thumb. The crest stops being enormous. It had nothing left to be big against. Public domain.


Working space versus an under-filled frame
This is the distinction that matters most when you are judging images, and it is the one people fudge. Both look "empty". They are not the same.
Negative space is doing work when:

it has a shape you could describe (a wedge, an arc, a long horizontal band)
it isolates something, or points at something, or holds down the light side of an asymmetric Balance
taking it away would change what the image says

The frame is simply under-filled when:

the empty region has no shape, no gradient and no edge worth looking at
the subject would survive an aggressive crop with nothing lost
the space appeared because the photographer stood too far back, not because they wanted it

There is also a specific failure worth naming: trapped space. A pocket of emptiness sealed off between objects, unable to connect to the rest of the space in the frame — the gap between an arm and a torso, a slot between two buildings. It reads as dead, and it attracts attention it has not earned (SRC-029).
Across different media

Painting and print. Japanese woodblock prints and traditional ink painting leave large areas untouched on purpose; the blank paper is the mist, the water, the sky.
Design. Expensive brands use more space, discount retailers pack the shelf. The space itself communicates cost (SRC-029).
Film and 3D. Minimalist film posters survive on negative space alone — a handful of shapes, and the gaps carry the recognition. Brejon uses them as the clearest teaching examples for figure/ground he knows (SRC-098).

Common mistakes

"Empty space is wasted space, so crop tighter." Cropping tight is a decision with consequences: you remove the breathing room, you raise the tension, and you often destroy the subject's direction. Sometimes right, never automatic.
"Negative space means white or plain." It means whatever your eye reads as ground. Dense foliage, a textured brick wall, deep shadow and heavy blur all work as negative space when they carry no detail worth stopping on (SRC-024).
"More space always feels more sophisticated." Space with no shape is just an under-filled frame at a larger size.
"The background is not part of the composition." It is half of it, and it is the half that decides whether your subject reads as a figure at all.


Reading the empty half

Squint and name the shape of the largest empty region. If you cannot describe it in three words, nobody composed it.
Is the subject facing or moving somewhere? Is there space in that direction?
Look for space trapped between objects with no way out.
Cover the empty area with your hand. Does the picture get better, or does the subject suddenly feel cramped?
Ask which region your eye calls "the object". If it picks the background, the figure/ground split has gone the wrong way.
